meta.title: Still in View
meta.description: Compare lunar landing sites and dates: where the Sun and Earth are relative to the horizon.
app.name: Still in View
app.event: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 entry · Challenge: Lunar Landing Site Navigator
app.status: Pick one or more landing sites and UTC dates and times. Each answer says whether the Sun is above the horizon (solar power generation potential) and whether Earth is above it (direct-to-Earth communication), and for how long. What is built and its limitations: About.
footer.si: Built with SI (Claude Code, Anthropic) on the author's instructions.
tool.heading: Compare landing sites and dates
tool.intro: Pick a landing site and a date and time (UTC). Each scenario shows where the Sun and Earth are relative to the horizon. Sun above the horizon: solar power generation is possible. Earth above the horizon: direct-to-Earth communication is possible.
tool.data_label: Sun and Earth positions: precomputed from JPL Horizons (NASA JPL). Horizon: local terrain from LRO LOLA where the south polar elevation grids used here cover the site; elsewhere an ideal sphere horizon. Each scenario says which one it uses. Own coordinates: computed in browser, validated against JPL Horizons.

sky.aria: Horizon panorama. Sun: azimuth {saz}°, elevation {sel}°. Earth: azimuth {eaz}°, elevation {eel}°.
sky.terrain: Solid line = terrain skyline (LRO LOLA); dashed = ideal sphere horizon
horizon.terrain: Horizon: local terrain from LRO LOLA elevation data.
horizon.sphere: Horizon: ideal sphere horizon. Local terrain is not included (this site is outside the LOLA south polar grids used here).
details.data: Positions are read from an hourly JPL Horizons table computed for this site (observer on the lunar surface) and linearly interpolated between hours.
details.horizon: Above the horizon means elevation greater than {threshold}° against an ideal sphere horizon. Local terrain is not included for this site: it lies outside the LRO LOLA south polar elevation grids used here (75°S to the pole).
details.horizon_terrain: Above the horizon means the elevation is more than {threshold}° above the terrain skyline in that direction. The skyline is computed from LRO LOLA south polar elevation grids (80 m and 240 m per pixel) for an observer {h} m above the surface, measured from the same ideal-sphere reference as the JPL Horizons angles. Sunrise, sunset, Earthrise and Earthset use this skyline.
details.scale: Panorama: azimuth 0–360° left to right; elevation ±{scale}°, the same scale on every scenario.
details.windows: Sunrise, sunset, Earthrise and Earthset are where the interpolated elevation crosses the horizon threshold. A window that runs past the start or end of the precomputed table is shown as "at least" that long.
state.out_of_range: No precomputed data for this time. Available: {start} to {end} UTC.
state.load_error: Could not load the data for this site.

val.title: Validation — Still in View
val.description: How closely the Sun and Earth angles shown by this tool match JPL Horizons.
val.heading: Validation
val.intro: Do the angles this tool shows match JPL Horizons? Site-and-time pairs were drawn at random (fixed seed), never on a table hour, so they test the hourly interpolation. For each pair, the angles shown by this tool's own code are compared with JPL Horizons asked directly for the same site and minute.
val.not_checked: Terrain horizon: checked below against an independent NASA product (average Sun and Earth visibility maps).
val.generated: Measured {at} by scripts/validate.py (random seed {seed}). Source file: data/validation.json.
val.pgda.heading: Terrain horizon against NASA PGDA
val.pgda.intro: The terrain skyline is checked against an independent NASA product: the average Sun and Earth visibility maps of the lunar south pole (E. Mazarico, NASA GSFC PGDA; LOLA grid, {m} m per pixel). A map value is the share of hourly steps over 18.6 years when any part of the Sun or Earth disc was visible. This tool's value is the share of hours in its own table ({start} to {stop} UTC) when any part of the disc is above its terrain skyline. The periods differ, so the numbers are not expected to match exactly.
val.pgda.window: PGDA range nearby = lowest and highest map value in the {n} × {n} pixels around the point; it shows how fast the value changes within a few hundred metres.
val.pgda.source: Source: NASA GSFC PGDA, Lunar Polar Illumination
val.pgda.generated: Measured {at} by scripts/pgda.py. Source file: data/validation.json.
tl.heading: One lunar day
tl.intro: Sun and Earth elevation above the horizon over 29.5 Earth days around the chosen time (one lunar day). Lines above the horizon line = in view. The bars under the chart mark when each one is in view.
tl.lanes: Upper bar: Sun in view · lower bar: Earth in view
tl.intro_year: Sun and Earth elevation above the horizon over the whole one-year data table (hourly steps). Lines above the horizon line = in view. The bars under the chart mark when each one is in view.
tl.year_share: Over the whole table ({hours} hourly steps): Sun at least partly above the horizon {sun} % of the hours, Earth {earth} %.
tl.aria: Timeline from {from} to {to} UTC. Sun above the horizon {sun}% of the time, Earth above the horizon {earth}% of the time. Vertical scale ±{scale}°.
custom.hint: Decimal degrees: latitude {latMin} to {latMax} (south is negative); west longitudes may be typed as negative numbers. Computed in browser, validated against JPL Horizons; ideal sphere horizon only.
custom.name: Own point ({lat}°, {lon}° E)
custom.invalid.lat: Latitude must be a number from {min}° to {max}°.
custom.invalid.lon: Longitude must be a number from {min}° to {max}° (east positive).
custom.computing: Computing Sun and Earth positions in your browser…
horizon.custom: Horizon: ideal sphere horizon. Local terrain is not computed for own coordinates.
details.data_custom: Positions are computed in browser, validated against JPL Horizons: Astronomy Engine (MIT license) gives the Sun and Earth directions and the Moon's IAU rotation model on an hourly grid over the same dates as the precomputed tables, linearly interpolated between hours. The measured differences from JPL Horizons are on the Validation page.
details.horizon_custom: Above the horizon means elevation greater than {threshold}° against an ideal sphere horizon (radius {r} km). Local terrain is not computed for own coordinates, even inside the LRO LOLA grids.
val.engine.heading: Own coordinates: computed in browser, validated against JPL Horizons
val.engine.intro: For own coordinates the page computes the Sun and Earth angles itself (Astronomy Engine) on the same hourly grid and interpolates them the same way. The engine was run at the listed-site pairs above and at {n} unnamed check points (not landing sites) spread over the near side, far side and both poles, and compared with JPL Horizons asked directly.
val.engine.generated: Measured {at} by scripts/validate.py --engine (random seed {seed}). Source file: data/validation.json.
shift.heading: Small shifts in location or date
shift.intro: The same two answers when the time moves a little, or the point moves {km} km. Numbers = degrees above (+) or below (−) the horizon used for this scenario.
shift.changed: {n} of {total} shifts change at least one answer.
shift.place_computing: Computing the nearby points in your browser…
shift.place_source: Nearby points: terrain horizon from LRO LOLA (same method as this site). Sun and Earth positions there: computed in browser, validated against JPL Horizons.
shift.place_none: Location shifts are shown where a LOLA terrain horizon exists. On the ideal sphere, moving {km} km tilts the horizon by only {deg}°.
shift.place_error: Nearby points could not be computed.

surface.heading: Surface around the site (3D)
surface.intro: The same LOLA heights as the 2D map, {w} × {w} km, seen from above at an angle. Heights are stretched {x} times so the relief is visible.
surface.aria: Surface of heights, {w} × {w} km around the site, looking toward azimuth {deg}°. {sun}. {earth}.

surface.dir_earth: Earth at the chosen time: azimuth {az}°, elevation {el}°
surface.stretch: The Sun and Earth lines start at the site. Their upward part is stretched like the heights, so they look steeper than they are. Dashed line = below the horizon at the chosen time. The lines are drawn on top of the ground.
surface.shading: Relief shading uses the same fixed light as the 2D map. It is not the real Sun and shows no shadows.

about.title: About — Still in View
about.description: What Still in View shows, item by item, and its limitations.
about.heading: About this tool
about.quote: “Your challenge is to create an intuitive tool or application that lets mission planners, educators, and the public compare landing sites and dates quickly, visualizing Sun and Earth positions relative to the horizon to assess power generation potential and direct-to-Earth communication windows.”
about.quote_source: — challenge text, NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, Lunar Landing Site Navigator
about.audiences: I chose all three audiences named in the challenge (mission planners, educators, the public) and all twelve items in the challenge's “Your solution may include” list. One tool serves all three: plain answers first, technical details one click away.
about.items.heading: What it shows, item by item
about.item.a_known_sites: Known landing sites: all six Apollo landings, CLPS IM-1 and IM-2, Chandrayaan-3 and Chang'e 4, each coordinate copied from a cited NASA page (NSSDCA or LROC).
about.item.b_custom_coordinates: Own coordinates: any latitude and longitude on the Moon. Sun and Earth positions are computed in browser (Astronomy Engine), validated against JPL Horizons.
about.item.c_compare: Compare: up to {max} scenarios at once, as cards and in one side-by-side table.
about.item.d_date_time: Date and time: any UTC date and time from {start} to {stop}; the timeline shows how the Sun and Earth move through one lunar day.
about.item.e_time_remaining: Time remaining before sunset or Earthset, or until sunrise or Earthrise.
about.item.f_key_numbers: Key numbers: Sun elevation angle, duration of sunlight and the Earth visibility window around the chosen time.
about.item.g_timeline: Timeline of one lunar day (29.5 Earth days): Sun and Earth elevation over time, bars for when each is in view, a slider and a Play button (hidden when the device asks for reduced motion).
about.item.h_map_2d: 2D map of LRO LOLA heights around each terrain site, with the site and the Sun and Earth directions at the chosen time.
about.item.i_surface_3d: 3D surface of the same LOLA heights; it can be turned to look in any direction, and its heights are stretched.
about.item.j_terrain_horizon: Local terrain horizon from LRO LOLA at the south polar sites inside the elevation grids used here; every other site uses the ideal sphere horizon and says so.
about.item.k_moon_vs_earth: Moon and Earth compared: length of one day, how fast the Sun moves across the sky, surface air pressure and distance to the horizon, with values quoted from the NASA NSSDCA Moon and Earth fact sheets.
about.item.l_small_shifts: Small shifts in location or date: the same two answers for the chosen time moved 6 hours and 1 day either way and, at the terrain sites, for points 1 km north, east, south and west.
about.lims.heading: Limitations
about.lims.intro: What the tool does not do, by item where it applies.
about.lim.1_dates: Dates (d): the Sun and Earth tables cover {start} to {stop} UTC only, one row per hour, interpolated in between.
about.lim.2_terrain: Terrain horizon (j): only at IM-1 and IM-2, the listed sites inside the LOLA south polar grids used here (75°S to the pole). Every other listed site uses the ideal sphere horizon.
about.lim.3_own: Own coordinates (b): ideal sphere horizon only. Local terrain is not computed for own coordinates, even inside the LOLA grids.
about.lim.4_local: 2D map (h), 3D surface (i) and the 1 km location shifts (l): only at IM-1 and IM-2. Other sites show the date shifts only.
about.lim.5_surface: 3D surface (i): the Sun and Earth lines are drawn on top of the ground; terrain does not hide them, and no shadows are drawn.
about.lim.6_disc: In view means the centre of the Sun or Earth disc is above the horizon; a partly risen disc counts as not in view. The independent terrain check on the Validation page counts any part of the disc, and its differences are shown there.
about.lim.7_geometry: Power and communication answers are geometry only: whether the Sun or Earth is above the horizon. Solar panel orientation, power output, antennas, relay satellites and link budgets are not modelled.
about.lim.8_language: The interface is in English only.
about.si.heading: How SI was used
about.si.author: Decided by the author: to take part, the Jakarta event, this challenge, the audiences and the items to build, chosen from the list in NASA's challenge text.
about.si.tool: Done by SI (Claude Code, Anthropic), on the author's instructions: a feasibility comparison of the challenges, translation of the challenge text into Malay for the author, build order, interface design, all code and data scripts, tests, slide layout, and translating and editing the author's Malay notes into English text.
about.si.none: Not used: no SI-generated images, video or audio. Full details: SI disclosure (link below).

play.title: Play: Sun and Earth above the horizon · Still in View
play.description: A short game with the same answers as the Compare tool: one landing site and one UTC time per round, two yes/no questions.
play.heading: Sun and Earth: above the horizon or not?
play.intro: Each round shows one landing site and one UTC time. Answer the two questions the Compare tool answers, then press Check. The answers come from the same frozen JPL Horizons tables and horizons as the tool (LRO LOLA terrain skyline where the site has one, ideal sphere elsewhere).
play.q_power: Sunlight for solar power? (Sun above the horizon)
play.q_comm: Direct line to Earth? (Earth above the horizon)
play.reason_terrain: {body} elevation {el}° at azimuth {az}°; the terrain skyline in that direction is at {sky}°, so the {body} is {margin}° {dir} it.
play.reason_sphere: {body} elevation {el}° at azimuth {az}°; the ideal sphere horizon is at 0°, so the {body} is {margin}° {dir} it.
play.sky_aria: Horizon panorama for this round, elevation ±{scale}°: Sun and Earth markers, solid when above the horizon used, hollow when below.
play.open: Open this scenario in the tool
play.score_note: Every answer was computed from the same tables and horizons as the Compare tool, with the centre of the Sun or Earth disc above the horizon used.
